text: Write the four obligations check: a subclass that widens what it accepts is safe. Fill in the two blanks.
choices: static class Base { void record(int amount) {
static class Wider extends Base { @Override void record(int amount) {
if (___) System.out.println("wider recorded " + amount);   // accepts negatives too
new Wider().record(-5);             // legal: preconditions may be weakened
// a subclass calling ___ would keep the parent's stricter rule
explanation: Verified: `wider recorded -5` then `base recorded 5`. Accepting more is safe because every call valid against the supertype remains valid — preconditions may be weakened, never strengthened. Postconditions run the opposite way: they may be strengthened, never weakened. Java enforces only the fifth, mechanical rule, that access may not be narrowed, and leaves the other four to you.
